newsitem.title: UK: Metals Outlook - Players sift clues for copper future.
newsitem.headline: Metals Outlook - Players sift clues for copper future.

text.p: Copper remains tight in the short term, buoyed by eroding stocks and supply hiccups, analysts said.
But market players attending an industry gathering in Spain this week will be debating whether prices can build a solid foundation on last week's heady gains.
With a major aluminium conference and a tin gathering also due this week, trading numbers may be depleted as the May contract matures on the London Metal Exchange later on Monday.
Three months LME copper surged on Friday to a near one-year high of $2,488 per tonne, a jump of almost $100 on the week.

At last week's peak, copper had climbed by $340 or about 16 percent so far this year, moving back to the region it saw nearly a year ago, before huge trading losses by Sumitomo sparked a meltdown in prices and rattled confidence.
On Friday afternoon profit-taking trimmed gains and copper closed at $2,466.
"Investors naturally query how much more upside there is to the fabulous copper price," said analyst Nick Moore of Flemings Global Mining Group.

"For investors with the whole panorama of metals from which to choose, it all seems to boil down to a question of confidence," he said. Moore recommended base metal exposure should be skewed to aluminium, zinc and nickel.
In the short term, many traders believe copper prices have further to go, even if corrections are needed from time to time as overbought signals flash.
Analyst Martin Squires of broker Rudolf Wolff said a bullish flag pattern targetted $2,600 while broker Brandeis said a reverse head-and-shoulders implied a move to $2,630.

At Friday's close, prices were still looking a little overheated with the Relative Strength Index over the 70 percent benchmark at 73. Any pullback should find support at $2,433/40, the breakout point for the recent move.

LME stocks started to erode again last week after showing some increases in the wake of a $200 cash/threes backwardation seen in late April. By Friday, inventories were down during the week by 9,675 tonnes to 143,675 tonnes. Consumer offtake is strong and some traders expect another 10,000-tonne drawdown this week after Monday's draw of 2,100 tonnes.
Severe weather has trimmed output in Chile, where labour unrest also threatens the sector in the near term.
But the longer term outlook is sure to spark heated debate between bulls and bears at Metal Bulletin's International Copper Conference in Seville, Spain kicking off on Monday.
Bankers Trust recently put out a bullish report that saw prices soaring to $1.30 cents/lb ($2,866 per tonne) by the end of the year on Chinese demand, which it deemed had been underestimated.
But others believe a long-awaited surplus will begin to appear in the later half of the year.
In addition, Kennecott Copper's Garfield smelter will be back on line next month after a maintenance shutdown which is supposed to put an end to months of difficulties at the new plant.
"The market should prepare itself for a significant pick-up in refined production in the second half of the year," Squires said.
The plant only produced 53,800 tonnes last year compared with planned output of 285,000 tonnes.

"Despite the impending impact of the re-introduction of this and new capacity coming on stream, the market remains vulnerable to upside spikes, with the uncertainty surrounding the Chinese and their import requirements," Squires added in a commentary.
The aluminium market will be thinner this week as over 2,000 industry participants head to Atlanta, Georgia for the Alumitech '97 conference, which starts on Tuesday.
Speakers at the event include the chairmen of Alumax Inc, Kaiser Aluminum Corp and Reynolds Metals Co.

The aluminium price moved sideways last week after breaking above $1,650 the week before. It topped out last Monday at $1,679 but ran into producer selling each time it tried to move back towards that area, ending on Friday at $1,666.50.
The market may need a rest before re-challenging the $1,700 area seen in early March, analysts said.
In Brussels, the International Tin Research Institute is holding the World Tin Conference, which opens on Tuesday.
